quote: I'm interested, but I know they're very expensive. So if if this is gonna be very expensive, you could just take me off the list.
stewart_read: This is a textbook trigger for the 'too expensive' flip — Donna states cost fear before any pitch. Rep instead reassures with a generic no-upfront-cost line rather than reframing her existing ~$300 bill (captured moments later) as the actual expense.
alternative_hypothesis: Rep may have been sequencing deliberately — reassure first, gather the bill number later, flip afterward. But no flip ever occurs after the bill is captured at 03:24, so the sequencing theory doesn't hold up.
coaching_implication: Coach the rep to hold the bill number back mentally through the objection, then use it explicitly: 'You're already paying $300 a month — that's the real expense, solar is just replacing it.'

stewart_read: Bill captured (~$300/month) inside the first 4 minutes, which meets the schema's capture-speed bar, but the rep files it ('That is good to know') without flipping it into emotional leverage.
coaching_implication: This is the moment to loop back to her earlier expense fear from 02:34 explicitly — capture alone isn't the win, the flip is.

quote: Yeah. And it was I remember it being very, very expensive. Mhmm. And, so I just kinda let it go
stewart_read: The same cost fear resurfaces in past-tense form. Rep pivots to 'technology has improved' framing, which is a feature-explanation deflection rather than tying the improvement back to her current $300 bill as proof the math has changed for her specifically.
alternative_hypothesis: Rep could be strategically avoiding re-litigating cost twice in one call to keep momentum toward bill collection — but there's no evidence of a planned callback to the point later in the call, so this reads as a missed rather than deferred opportunity.
coaching_implication: When the same fear repeats, that's the signal to use the customer's own number as proof, not to reach for a generic 'things have changed' line.

quote: Well, I'm from New Mexico, and, they're saying that they're giving a lot of incentives for solar panels.
stewart_read: Donna hands the rep a usable anchor (state incentive interest) but the rep's very next line jumps straight into the cost reassurance without expanding on or validating her incentive-driven motivation — the schema calls for 60+ seconds of depth here, and this exchange runs about 10 seconds before pivoting.
coaching_implication: Coach the rep to ask a genuine follow-up ('What have you heard about the incentives?') to deepen the interest-anchor before racing into qualifiers — this creates curiosity and buys more rapport before the cost objection even surfaces.

quote: Do you happen to have an online account with them by any chance?
stewart_read: When Donna reveals she's away from home until Monday and has no online account, the rep pivots within seconds to a texted-link/photo-later fallback rather than pressing or burning call time — a clean, schema-aligned quick pivot well under the 2-minute friction budget.
coaching_implication: This is a positive, replayable moment — hold it up as an example of efficient bill-collection triage when the ideal path (mail bill, in-hand) isn't available.

stewart_read: The call ends with no locked appointment day/time, no 'is that fair?' handshake, and no stated next step owned by the rep beyond a vague promise to try to call Monday. This is procedural fragility, not a real customer barrier.
coaching_implication: Coach the rep to convert the Monday bill-callback into an actual scheduled time slot with the closer — 'Once I get that photo Monday, I'll have you on the calendar with our consultant at [time]' — rather than leaving it as an informal follow-up.
